examples.problem_statement: Write the equation of the line which passes through the point of intersection of the lines l₁: 3x + 5y + 29 = 0 and l₂: 7x - 11y - 13 = 0 and through the point (2, 1).

solution.operation: Form family of lines through intersection
solution.description: Any line through the intersection of l1 and l2 can be written as l1 plus k times l2, so build the family 3x + 5y + 29 + k(7x - 11y - 13) = 0. One unknown k now stands in for every such line, and the intersection point itself never has to be computed.
The wanted line also passes through (2, 1), so those coordinates must satisfy the family equation. Substituting x = 2 and y = 1 turns the family into a single equation whose only unknown is k.
Work out the arithmetic on each side of the parameter: the plain part gives 6 + 5 + 29 = 40 and the bracket gives 14 - 11 - 13 = -10, so the condition collapses to 40 - 10k = 0.
Solve that linear equation for the parameter. Moving 10k across and dividing by 10 gives k = 4, the single member of the family that passes through (2, 1).

solution.operation: Substitute k=4 back into family equation
solution.description: Put k = 4 back into the family to select the one line wanted: 3x + 5y + 29 + 4(7x - 11y - 13) = 0.
Distribute the 4 through the bracket and collect like terms: 3x + 28x gives 31x, 5y - 44y gives -39y, and 29 - 52 gives -23, leaving the standard form 31x - 39y - 23 = 0.
Check the finished equation against the point it was built for. Substituting (2, 1) gives 62 - 39 - 23 = 0, so the point does lie on the line and the value of k was right.

{'point': 'Note: The point (2,1) is not on l₂, so the family l₁ + kl₂ includes the desired line.'}
{'point': 'Caution: The line l₂ itself is excluded from the family l₁ + kl₂.'}
{'point': 'Speed tip: Use the parameterized form directly to avoid solving simultaneous equations for intersection point.'}

Sign slips while collecting like terms, especially 5y - 44y and 29 - 52.
Solving l1 and l2 simultaneously for the intersection point first, which is exactly the work this family method is designed to avoid.

examples.problem_statement: Insert four geometric means between 25 and $\frac{1}{125}$.

solution.description: Read the two endpoints from the problem: the progression starts at 25 and ends at 1/125. Four means are to sit between them, so the finished progression has six terms in all.

In a geometric progression each term is the previous one times a fixed ratio, so the last term of an n-term progression is the first term times the ratio raised to the power n minus 1. With four means inserted, n is 6 and the exponent will be 5.
Substitute the known values into that formula: first term 25, last term 1/125 and n = 6 give 1/125 = 25 times r to the fifth power.

Divide both sides by 25 to isolate the power. The right side becomes 1 over 125 times 25, which is 1 over 3125, and since 3125 is 5 multiplied by itself five times this is exactly one fifth raised to the fifth power.
Both sides are now fifth powers, so take the fifth root of each. The common ratio is 1/5.
Generate the means by multiplying repeatedly by the ratio 1/5: 25 gives 5, then 5 gives 1, then 1 gives 1/5, then 1/5 gives 1/25. These four values are the requested geometric means.
Write the whole progression out and check the end: one more multiplication by 1/5 takes 1/25 to 1/125, the last term given in the problem, confirming both the ratio and the means.

{'point': 'The sign to be used is the common sign of $a$ and $l$.'}

Computing 125 times 25 as 3025 rather than 3125, which destroys the clean fifth root.
Taking the fifth root of 1/3125 by dividing rather than by recognising it as a fifth power, for instance writing r = 1/625.

examples.problem_statement: From the table of values of $(\frac{1}{2})^n$ in Table 13.1, it appears that, as $n$ increases indefinitely, $(\frac{1}{2})^n$ decreases indefinitely while remaining positive. Moreover, it can be made to have a value as near 0 as we please by choosing $n$ sufficiently large. We describe this state of affairs by saying: The limit of $(\frac{1}{2})^n$, as $n$ increases indefinitely, is 0.

solution.description: Compute the first few powers of one half: 0.5, then 0.25, 0.125 and 0.0625. Each value is smaller than the one before, yet every one of them is still greater than zero, which is the pattern the rest of the argument has to pin down.
Rewrite the power of one half as 1 divided by 2 to the n. In this form the numerator is fixed at 1 while the denominator doubles at every step, which is why the values shrink.
State the question as a limit: what value does 1 over 2 to the n approach as n increases without bound? The two forms are the same expression, so either may be used.

Set out the formal test for the limit being zero. Given any positive tolerance epsilon, however small, there must exist a cut-off N such that every n beyond N makes 1 over 2 to the n smaller than that tolerance.

Show such an N always exists by solving the inequality for n. Requiring 1 over 2 to the n to be below epsilon means 2 to the n must exceed 1 over epsilon, so any n larger than the base-two logarithm of 1 over epsilon works, and N can be the next whole number above it.
Because a suitable N can be produced for every epsilon, the values can be forced as close to zero as anyone demands, which is precisely what it means for the limit to be 0.

examples.answer: The limit of $(\frac{1}{2})^n$, as $n$ increases indefinitely, is 0.

examples.problem_statement: For the infinite geometric series $12 + 4 + \frac{4}{3} + \frac{4}{9} + \cdots$, find the sum.

solution.description: Look at how each term arises from the one before it. Going 12 to 4 to 4/3 to 4/9, every step multiplies by the same number, which identifies the series as geometric rather than arithmetic.
Read the first term straight off the series: a is 12.
Divide any term by the one before it to get the common ratio: 4 divided by 12 is 1/3. Checking a second pair, 4/3 divided by 4 is also 1/3, so the ratio is genuinely constant.

Test convergence before summing. An infinite geometric series has a finite sum only when the absolute value of the ratio is below 1; here it is 1/3, so the series converges and the sum formula may be used.

solution.operation: Apply the sum formula for an infinite geometric series
solution.description: Bring in the formula for the sum of a convergent infinite geometric series: the first term divided by one minus the ratio.
Substitute the two quantities already found, a = 12 and r = 1/3, giving 12 divided by the quantity one minus one third.
Simplify: the denominator one minus one third is two thirds, and dividing by two thirds means multiplying by three halves, so 12 times 3/2 gives 18.
State the result: the infinite series sums to 18.

examples.problem_statement: Find the limiting value of the repeating decimal $0.727272\ldots$.

solution.description: Split the repeating decimal into the blocks that repeat. The pair 72 recurs, so 0.727272... is 0.72 + 0.0072 + 0.000072 and so on, an infinite geometric series rather than an endless decimal.

Read the two quantities that series needs: the first block is 0.72, and each block is one hundredth of the previous one because the repeating pair shifts two places right each time, so the ratio is 0.01.
The ratio is far below 1 in absolute value, so apply the infinite sum formula: 0.72 divided by one minus 0.01, which is 0.72 over 0.99.
Clear the decimals by scaling both parts by 100 to get 72 over 99, then divide numerator and denominator by their common factor 9 to reach 8/11, the exact value of the repeating decimal.

examples.problem_statement: Observe the sum of the first n odd integers for n = 1, 2, 3, 4.

solution.description: Start with the smallest case. For n = 1 there is only one odd number, 1, and 1 is also 1 squared, so the sum matches the square at the first case.
Take two odd numbers: 1 + 3 is 4, and 4 is 2 squared, so the pattern survives the second case.
Take three: 1 + 3 + 5 is 9, which is 3 squared. The running total is again the square of how many terms were added.
Take four: 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 is 16, which is 4 squared, a fourth case agreeing with the same rule.

Read the common shape of the four observations. The nth odd number is 2n - 1, and each running total was the square of the count, so the conjecture is that the odd numbers up to 2n - 1 sum to n squared. Four cases suggest this; they do not prove it.
Begin the proof properly by fixing the base case: at n = 1 the sum is 1 and n squared is 1, exactly the check already made in step 1.

Assume the formula holds for one particular positive integer k, so the odd numbers up to 2k - 1 add to k squared. This assumption is the inductive hypothesis, and it is assumed for a single k rather than for all n.
Add the next odd number, 2(k + 1) - 1 = 2k + 1, to both sides. The right side becomes k squared plus 2k plus 1, which is (k + 1) squared, so truth at k forces truth at k + 1 and the induction closes.

examples.problem_statement: Observe the number of lines determined by n points (where no 3 points are collinear) for n = 2, 3, 4, 5.

solution.description: Count the lines for each of the small cases named in the problem, taking the points in general position so no three lie on one line. Comparing the counts as n runs 2, 3, 4, 5 exposes a regular pattern, which is the observation the exercise is built on and which leads to the half n times n minus 1 rule.

examples.problem_statement: Test the hypothesis that f(n) = n^4/8 - 17n^3/12 + 47n^2/8 - 103n/12 + 6 is a prime number for every positive integral value of n.

solution.description: Evaluate the polynomial at the first few positive integers and note that the values that come out are prime. These agreeable early cases are exactly what makes the hypothesis tempting.

Keep testing beyond the cases that agree instead of stopping there. At n = 6 the polynomial gives 22, which is 2 times 11 and therefore not prime, and one counterexample is enough to destroy the claim.

examples.answer: The conclusion is false since f(6) = 22 is not a prime number.

solution.description: Check the smallest case first. At n = 1 the left side holds only the single term 2 times 1 minus 1, which is 1, and the right side is 1 squared, also 1, so the base case is verified.

Assume the formula is true for one particular positive integer k, so the odd numbers up to 2k - 1 sum to k squared. This is the inductive hypothesis; nothing is proved here, it is the thing the next step will lean on.
Move to the next case, n = k + 1. The odd number that has to be added is 2(k + 1) - 1, which is 2k + 1, so the sum for k + 1 is the bracketed sum up to 2k - 1 with 2k + 1 appended.
Replace that bracketed sum with k squared, which is exactly what the inductive hypothesis permits. The expression becomes k squared plus 2k + 1.
Recognise k squared plus 2k plus 1 as the perfect square (k + 1) squared, which is what the formula predicts for n = k + 1, so the step from k to k + 1 is complete.
With the base case verified and the step from k to k + 1 established, the principle of mathematical induction carries the formula to every positive integer n.

examples.problem_statement: Expand $(3x + 2y^2)^5$ and simplify term by term.

solution.description: Match the expression to the binomial theorem by naming its parts: a is 3x, b is 2y squared, and n is 5. The expansion will therefore be a sum of six terms, each a binomial coefficient times a power of 3x times a power of 2y squared.

solution.operation: Write out each term using binomial coefficients
solution.description: Write out those six terms in order, letting the exponent on 3x fall from 5 down to 0 while the exponent on 2y squared rises from 0 up to 5, with the matching coefficient in front of each.
Evaluate the six coefficients from n factorial over k factorial times n minus k factorial, giving the symmetric row 1, 5, 10, 10, 5, 1.

Simplify each term on its own, raising the numerical parts to their powers as well as the letters: 3 to the fifth is 243, 5 times 81 times 2 is 810, 10 times 27 times 4 is 1080, 10 times 9 times 8 is 720, 5 times 3 times 16 is 240, and 2 to the fifth is 32. The terms are 243x^5, 810x^4y^2, 1080x^3y^4, 720x^2y^6, 240xy^8 and 32y^10.
Add the six simplified terms in the order they were generated to write the expansion as a single polynomial.

solution.operation: Verify no like terms to combine
solution.description: Scan the finished expansion for like terms. Every term carries a different pair of exponents on x and y, so none combine and the expression is already fully simplified.
